The impact of nonvisual effects of daylight on building occupants:
Implications on lighting standards and human centric lighting design
A thesis submitted in fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of
Doctor of Philosophy
by

“Without metrics that relate to human response we have no useful measure of the
effectiveness of lighting.
Without a measure of the effectiveness of lighting we have no valid measure of the efficiency
of lighting.”
Christopher (Kit) Cuttle
PhD FSLL FIESANZ FIESNA

i

Abstract
The use of light in a building is often treated as a functional requirement rather than a
combination of function, health and well-being. Existing lighting standards focus on visual
performance and comfort, which has a direct effect on the health and well-being of building
occupants; they nonetheless miss the critical role the non-visual effects of light play on
people’s overall response at present. In lighting standards, despite the acknowledged benefits
of daylighting, daylight is typically treated as a light source to minimise the use of electric
light, with openings for daylight penetration mostly regarded as access to views for building
occupants to connect to the outside. Critically, the science underpinning these standards is
almost a century old. The non-visual effects responsible for circadian, hormonal and
behavioural system regulation identified since the discovery of the intrinsically
photosensitive retinal ganglion cells in 2002 have not been accounted for in lighting
standards. This research investigated the extent to which building occupants’ sense of well-
being changed in response to varying daylight levels under Daylight and Daylight plus View
conditions and how these may affect lighting standards and daylighting design. The short
wavelength non-visual effect melanopic daylight equivalent illuminance (mel - EDI),
photopic illuminance and correlated colour temperature (CCT) were used to define the
lighting levels. The participants’ sense of well-being was assessed by psychological and
physiological measures. An online survey was conducted separately to collect further data on
building occupants’ lighting preferences. The laboratory cohort was comprised of 20 young
(27.3 ± 4.4 years old) and 18 elderly (74.2 ± 7.9 years old) adults. Significant associations
between light and heart rate variability (HRV) were found. The HF Power, which had a
strong association with calmness and heart rate reduction, F(1,69.1) = 7.63, p = 0.01, was
observed when the participants were exposed to bright outdoor daylight (HF outdoor: 31.0
nu
± 1.2 versus HF indoor: 30.2 ± 1.2). The HF power was found to be positively correlated
nu
with the light intensity, t(43.6) = -2.21, p = 0.03, supporting the hypothesis that an increase
in the level of sense of well-being accompanied the increase in lighting. There occurred no
difference in response between Daylight only and View conditions (p > 0.05) and also
between age groups (p > 0.05). The lighting measurements taken on the horizontal surface
(EH) varied significantly from those taken at eye level (E ), e.g., median at Baseline E =
V V
2,132 lx and E = 1,217 lx and t(65) = 2.84, p < 0.01. The online survey showed that
H
respondents were proportionally happier, Ρ(73) = 0.25, p = 0.03, more energetic, Ρ(73) =
ii

0.24, p = 0.04, and less tense, Ρ(73) = -0.30, p = 0.01, when they were satisfied with their
lighting environment. They were, however, less calm if deprived of access to natural light.
These results show that daylight, in addition to psychological, circadian, and hormone effects,
also affects HRV, giving further impetus for light standards to include non-visual effects as a
design consideration. The significant differences between E and E demonstrated that
V H
lighting standards should adopt CIE’s recommendation, The International Commission on
Illumination, of measuring light at eye level to maintain an accurate representation of the
amount of light incident on the observer’s eyes.
Given the complexity of human response and the number of variables involved in lighting
design, this thesis proposes an alternative lighting design framework. This framework, based
on existing processes, takes into account both visual and non-visual effects of light. It also
explores the potential of technology to facilitate the transition to the ‘melanopic age’ of
lighting design, a future where lighting standards are more comprehensive and considerate of
human well-being.
Keywords: daylighting design, intrinsically photosensitive ganglion cells (ipRGCs), lighting
design objectives (LiDOs), melanopic daylight equivalent illuminance (mel – EDI), mood,
nonvisual effects, stress

Chapter 1 Introduction
This chapter gives an overview of the research project, starting with the evolution of daylight
as the primary source of interior lighting to the almost universal use of artificial lights in
public and commercial buildings. It details the scope and rationale of this research project,
its significance and how achieving its objectives will address existing knowledge gaps and
advance lighting design that “integrate [the] thinking about light and lighting as mediators of
visual, biological and behavioural responses in humans.” - human centric lighting (Houser et
al. 2021).
1.1 The evolution of daylighting
All living organisms, including humans, have a biological clock. Diurnal animals require the
light-dark cycle to synchronise their master clock. Incorporating daylight into the built
environment, which supported the light-dark cycle by default, was the norm before the advent
of modern technologies. The earliest record attributed to Socrates (469 – 399 BC), pertaining
to daylighting design, was in Memorabilia by Xenophon (Xenophon & Dakyns 1998):
Now, supposing a house to have a southern aspect, sunshine during winter will steal in
under the verandah, but in summer, when the sun traverses a path right over our heads,
the roof will afford an agreeable shade, will it not? If, then, such an arrangement is
desirable, the southern side of a house should be built higher to catch the rays of the
winter sun, and the northern side lower to prevent the cold winds finding ingress; in a
word, it is reasonable to suppose that the pleasantest and most beautiful dwelling place
will be one in which the owner can at all seasons of the year find the pleasantest retreat,
and stow away his goods with the greatest security.
The communities of Olynthus and Priene reflected the Greeks’ belief in democratising
daylight access. The Romans legislated the right for the citizens to access daylight in their
buildings; solar rights were included in the Roman Justinian Code of Law (Lepore 2017).
Daylighting has been inextricably linked to the technological development of civilisation.
The development included structural engineering that reduced the reliance on outside walls
for support, enabling larger openings for bigger windows. Then came the Industrial
Revolution, which put pressure on designers and builders to quickly construct buildings to
house the migration of workers from the country to the city. This demand created houses
1

with small windows, with limited sunlight penetration, often built in crowded and unhealthy
conditions (Boubekri 2014). Prior to World War II, opening designs such as the sawtooth
roof allowed the plentiful ingress of daylight. The invention of electric light, air conditioning
and the development of high density buildings have further disrupted our exposure to the
natural light-dark cycle. The evolution of the workplace window design is clearly
demonstrated in Figure 1.1, Figure 1.2, and Figure 1.3. The size of the windows gradually
decreased as the use of artificial light gained popularity. In parallel, heating, ventilation and
air conditioning (HVAC) systems have replaced the need for openable windows for
ventilation. These innovations also allowed the increase of the floor plate area and the
decrease of floor to ceiling height, taking the building occupants further away from daylight
and the view from windows.

Figure 1.1: Mid 1800s Figure 1.2: Keesing Figure 1.3: 1967 Treasury
printing workshop. Technologies 1907 office. Reserve Office (pre-retrofit),

Until the 1940s, daylight remained the primary source of interior lighting, but since then,
building lighting requirements have mainly relied on electric lighting systems. One of the
main factors for this was the readily accessible electricity supply and the affordability of
electric light. Another reason was the need to minimise heat gain or loss by reducing the size
of the windows. Since electric lighting can meet most, if not all, occupants' functional
needs (Edwards & Torcellini 2002; Reinhart & Stein 2014), it was easy to adjust the window
size to accommodate HVAC loading requirements. Anecdotally, floor to ceiling glazing
appears to have gained popularity in commercial buildings in recent years, as shown in

windows in high density construction are other factors responsible for the transition from
daylight interior illumination to reliance on artificial lights. However, research consistently
shows that people prefer natural light and windows (Aries, Veitch & Newsham 2010; Farley
& Veitch 2001; Finnegan & Solomon 1981; Roche, Dewey & Littlefair 2000). This
phenomenon can largely be explained by studies on the importance of daylight exposure on
subjective mood change (Küller et al. 2006) and the restorative power of being able to see
outside (Berman, Jonides & Kaplan 2008; Kaplan & Kaplan 1989). In her book Healing
Spaces, Esther Sternberg postulates that this preference has an evolutionary origin (Sternberg
2009). There is also emerging research on the recognition of nonvisual effects of the short
wavelength violet-blue spectrum light on our circadian rhythms (Duffy & Czeisler 2009), in
addition to light’s capacity to increase alertness (Cajochen et al. 2000), mood (Wirz-Justice
2006), to affect hormone secretion (Lewy et al. 1980), and the need to maximise the use of
daylight instead of electric lights to reduce society's carbon emission to combat the effects of
climate change.

1.2 Designing for health: Effects of daylighting and views
Aside from the functional utility of daylight, daylighting is increasingly used for
psychological and physiological health reasons. Exploiting the benefits of daylight and
nature is not a modern phenomenon. The builders of the temples of Asclepius, the ancient
Greek god of healing, where the chronically or terminally ill visited in search of healing,
were built far away from towns and urban pollutants, always located near fresh water sources
and often with an aesthetic view and natural light (Devlin & Arneill 2003; Sternberg 2009).
